title: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access
content:
Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday.
The arrangement comes at a time where incidents of AI agents acting outside their instructions have been disclosed every week or two since late August. The incidents have sharpened calls for independent checks on AI companies.
“We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making,” Anthropic said in the blog post. “We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.”
Under the new arrangement, the METR team has Anthropic-issued company laptops, office space, and access to internal tools roughly on par with what Anthropic’s own risk assessment teams use. “Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk” the company said.
Anthropic compared the arrangement to banking, similar to how regulators place resident examiners inside the largest banks.
METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the company has given up the right to block them.
“Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, pre-defined categories,” the company said, such as customer data, anything attorney-client privileged, or relating to information about its model architectures. “METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information” Anthropic added.
METR is the only evaluator so far at the top of a three-tier system Anthropic is building. Evaluators in the bottom tier, like biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio, run narrow reviews and require Anthropic’s approval to publish. The middle tier gets more information and can publish without approval, while the top tier adds METR’s employee-level access.
Thursday’s announcement makes good on a promise Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made in a September essay, where he proposed embedding outside evaluators inside AI labs as a first step toward slowing the technology’s development. OpenAI quickly pledged the same, and both companies, along with Google, Meta, Nvidia, and xAI, have since signed a White House accord committing to independent review.

report.summary: Anthropic grants METR six researchers employee-level access to independently assess its frontier models, safety practices, and risk management, with limited redaction rights but no veto over publication.
report.background: The arrangement arrives after a wave of disclosures since late August in which AI agents acted outside their instructions, sometimes every week or two. Those incidents have intensified calls for independent scrutiny of frontier AI labs. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed embedding outside evaluators inside AI labs as a step toward safer development. OpenAI quickly pledged the same, and Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, Nvidia, and xAI later signed a White House accord committing to independent review. Anthropic is now building a three-tier evaluator system. METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier models, is the first and only evaluator at the top tier, granting it insider access akin to resident bank examiners. The experiment tests whether deep external access can build public trust without exposing customer data or core intellectual property.
key_points: METR's six researchers receive Anthropic-issued laptops, office space, and access to internal tools comparable to Anthropic's own risk assessment teams. Employees are encouraged to share information with them as they would with colleagues working on alignment risk. This lets METR independently assess Anthropic's models, safety practices, and risk management.

Anthropic cannot veto METR's publications, but it can require redactions in narrow, pre-defined categories such as customer data, attorney-client privileged material, and model architecture details. METR may publicly characterize the redactions and state whether it believes they were justified, without revealing the redacted information.

Anthropic is building a three-tier evaluator system. Bottom-tier evaluators like biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio run narrow reviews and need Anthropic's approval to publish. Middle-tier evaluators get more information and can publish without approval. Top-tier evaluators, currently only METR, add employee-level access.

The news follows weekly AI agent incidents since late August, growing demands for independent checks, Amodei's September essay, OpenAI's similar pledge, and a White House accord signed by major AI companies. It signals a shift from voluntary model cards to deeper operational transparency.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Anthropic's move sets a precedent for resident external evaluators, similar to bank examiners. If it works, other labs may face pressure to offer comparable access, reshaping how frontier risks are reviewed and disclosed. For developers, METR's assessments could clarify safety expectations, incident patterns, and deployment risks, influencing model releases and agent design. Regular users may gain more trustworthy evidence about model safety, but redactions on architecture and customer data limit full transparency. The arrangement is not regulation, and Anthropic controls access terms, so its credibility depends on METR's independence and publication record.
report.tools: Watch METR's public assessments and Task Standard, Anthropic's system cards and transparency reports, and the UK AI Safety Institute's Inspect framework for evaluations. Stanford HELM, OpenAI Evals, and Apollo Research's scheming evaluations offer related testing approaches. SecureBio covers biosecurity reviews. Developers can use these open tools to run structured safety and agentic risk tests, while tracking the three-tier evaluator list and any public redaction disputes.
